NOMINATION OF GUARDIAN FOR MINOR CHILDREN
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Riley Lee

NOMINATION DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, being the parent of Riley Lee, a minor child, hereby nominate Morgan Lee to serve as guardian of the person of Riley Lee. If Morgan Lee is unable, unwilling, or unavailable to serve, I nominate Casey Lee as guardian in their place. This nomination is made by written document as permitted under California law and is separate from any nomination made in a will.

NOMINATION BY WRITTEN DOCUMENT OUTSIDE A WILL
Jordan Alex Lee nominates Morgan Lee, and if that person is unable or unwilling to serve, Casey Lee, as guardian of the person of Riley Lee, by this written document. California Probate Code § 1500 permits a parent to nominate a guardian of a minor child's person or estate, or both. California Probate Code § 1502(a) permits that nomination to be made "in a writing signed either before or after the petition for the appointment of the guardian is filed" — meaning a signed nomination document can exist and take legal significance independent of a will and independent of an already-pending court case — and the same subsection directs a court to give the nomination "due weight," by cross-reference to Family Code § 3043.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to Section 1502, a parent may nominate a guardian of the person or estate, or both, of a minor child in either of the following cases: (a) Where the other parent nominates, or consents in writing to the nomination of, the same guardian for the same child. (b) Where, at the time the petition for appointment of the guardian is filed, either (1) the other parent is dead or lacks legal capacity to consent to the nomination or (2) the consent of the other parent would not be required for an adoption of the child."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1500 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1500 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1500)
  "A nomination of a guardian under this article may be made in the petition for the appointment of the guardian or at the hearing on the petition or in a writing signed either before or after the petition for the appointment of the guardian is filed. The court shall give due weight to the nomination of a guardian of the person pursuant to Section 3043 of the Family Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1502(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1502)
  "In determining the person or persons to whom custody should be granted under paragraph (2) or (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, the court shall consider and give due weight to the nomination of a guardian of the person of the child by a parent under Article 1 (commencing with Section 1500) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 4 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3043 (California Legislative Information text), the court's duty to give a guardian nomination due weight (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3043.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a parent's guardian nomination may be documented outside a will — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. Section 1500 itself is subject to Section 1502's conditions (e.g., when the other parent has not consented), and neither section makes a nomination self-executing; a court guardianship proceeding is still required to give it legal effect.

TIMING AND CONDITIONS OF A NOMINATION'S EFFECT
A nomination made under this document may be drafted to take effect immediately, or only upon the occurrence of a stated condition, such as Jordan Alex Lee's absence, travel, incapacity, or death. California Probate Code § 1502(b) allows a nomination in writing to specify the condition or conditions under which it becomes effective. Absent a contrary statement in the writing, § 1502(c) provides that a nomination remains effective notwithstanding the nominating parent's later absence, incapacity, or death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The nomination of a guardian under this article is effective when made except that a writing nominating a guardian under this article may provide that the nomination becomes effective only upon the occurrence of such condition or conditions as are specified in the writing, including, but not limited to, conditions as to the subsequent absence, legal incapacity, or death of the person making the nomination."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1502(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1502)
  "Unless the writing making the nomination expressly otherwise provides, a nomination made under this article remains effective notwithstanding the subsequent absence, legal incapacity, or death of the person making the nomination."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1502(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1502)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a written guardian nomination's timing and conditions can be structured — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1502); no additional independent source was found for this. A nomination's stated effective date or condition does not itself create a guardianship; a court proceeding is still the mechanism by which a guardian is actually appointed. Separately, Prob. Code § 1502(a) itself directs a court to give a parent's nomination "due weight" by cross-reference to Family Code § 3043 — a related fact addressed in this document's companion clause on standalone written nominations, not repeated here.

THE MINOR CHILD'S OWN ROLE IN A GUARDIANSHIP NOMINATION
Under California law, a minor who is 12 years of age or older may personally file a petition for the appointment of a guardian. In a proceeding to appoint a guardian of the person, the court is directed by Probate Code § 1514(b)(1) to the Family Code chapters governing custody of a minor, which include Family Code § 3042: where a child is of sufficient age and capacity to form an intelligent preference, the court must consider and give due weight to that preference, and a child 14 or older who wishes to address the court about the matter must be permitted to do so absent a contrary best-interest finding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older, may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian of the minor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510)
  "In appointing a guardian of the person, the court is governed by Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 3020) and Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3040) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code, relating to custody of a minor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1514(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1514)
  "If a child is of sufficient age and capacity to reason so as to form an intelligent preference as to custody or visitation, the court shall consider, and give due weight to, the wishes of the child in making an order granting or modifying custody or visitation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3042(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3042(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3042)
  "If the child is 14 years of age or older and wishes to address the court regarding custody or visitation, the child shall be permitted to do so, unless the court determines that doing so is not in the child’s best interest, in which case, the court shall state its reasons for that finding on the record."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3042(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3042(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3042)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a minor's own statutory role in who is nominated or appointed as their guardian — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. Family Code § 3042 is written for custody and visitation orders generally and is incorporated into guardian-of-the-person appointments only by Probate Code § 1514(b)(1)'s cross-reference to that Family Code chapter; it does not independently mention "guardian" nominations by name. A related, more directly on-point provision — Family Code § 3043, one section over — does require a court to give a parent's guardian nomination "due weight"; that provision is addressed in this document's companion clause on standalone written nominations.

THE CAREGIVER'S AUTHORIZATION AFFIDAVIT — WHAT IT ALLOWS WITHOUT COURT ACTION
California Family Code §§ 6550–6552 create a Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit that operates without any court proceeding. A caregiver 18 or older who completes items 1–4 of the statutory affidavit form and signs it is authorized to enroll Riley Lee in school and consent to school-related medical care. A caregiver who is a "relative" — defined by statute as an adult related to the child by blood, adoption, or affinity within the fifth degree of kinship, including stepparents, stepsiblings, and "great," "great-great," or "grand" relatives, or their spouses — who additionally completes items 5–8 and signs has the same rights to authorize medical and dental care given to guardians under Probate Code § 2353, which may include mental health treatment subject to the limits of Probate Code § 2356.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A caregiver’s authorization affidavit that meets the requirements of this part authorizes a caregiver 18 years of age or older who completes items 1 to 4, inclusive, of the affidavit provided in Section 6552 and signs the affidavit to enroll a minor in school and consent to school-related medical care on behalf of the minor. A caregiver who is a relative and who completes items 1 to 8, inclusive, of the affidavit provided in Section 6552 and signs the affidavit shall have the same rights to authorize medical care and dental care for the minor that are given to guardians under Section 2353 of the Probate Code. The medical care authorized by this caregiver who is a relative may include mental health treatment subject to the limitations of Section 2356 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 6550(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6550)
  "When signed by a relative, this affidavit shall confer the same rights to authorize medical care and dental care for the minor that are given to guardians under Section 2353 of the Probate Code. The medical care authorized by a relative caregiver may include mental health treatment subject to the limitations of Section 2356 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information), Fam. C. § 6552 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6552)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a no-court caregiver-authorization mechanism distinct from a court-appointed guardianship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The affidavit's authority to consent to medical/dental care beyond school-related care is available only to a caregiver who is a statutory "relative"; a non-relative caregiver's authority under this affidavit is limited to school enrollment and school-related medical care.

THE CAREGIVER'S AUTHORIZATION AFFIDAVIT — WHAT IT DOES NOT DO
The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit does not create a legal guardianship and does not affect the legal rights of Riley Lee's parents or legal guardian over the child's care, custody, and control. A caregiver's decision to consent to or refuse medical or dental care for the minor is superseded by any contravening decision of a parent or other person with legal custody, unless that decision would jeopardize the minor's life, health, or safety.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This declaration does not affect the rights of the minor’s parents or legal guardian regarding the care, custody, and control of the minor, and does not mean that the caregiver has legal custody of the minor."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information), Fam. C. § 6552 Notice 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6552)
  "The decision of a caregiver to consent to or to refuse medical or dental care for a minor shall be superseded by any contravening decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor, provided the decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor does not jeopardize the life, health, or safety of the minor."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 6550(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6550)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the stated limits of a no-court caregiver authorization — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. These are the limits stated in the cited text; the affidavit's interaction with a parent's or guardian's decision in a specific factual situation is not addressed further by these sections.

WHEN A CAREGIVER'S AUTHORIZATION AFFIDAVIT STOPS BEING VALID
The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit does not carry a fixed expiration date; instead, California Family Code § 6550(f) ties its validity to the minor's living arrangement. If Riley Lee stops living with the caregiver who signed the affidavit, that caregiver is required to notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that received the affidavit, and the affidavit becomes invalid once that notice is received.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If the minor stops living with the caregiver, the caregiver shall notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that has been given the affidavit. The affidavit is invalid after the school, health care provider, or health care service plan receives notice that the minor is no longer living with the caregiver."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(f) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 6550(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6550)
  "If the minor stops living with you, the affidavit is no longer valid. You are required to notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan to which you have given this affidavit that the minor is no longer living with you and that, as a result, the affidavit is no longer valid."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information), Fam. C. § 6552, To Caregivers ¶3 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6552)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a stated termination mechanism for a no-court caregiver authorization — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The statute ties invalidity to actual notice being received by the school or provider, not automatically to the date the child stops living with the caregiver.

THE AFFIDAVIT'S EFFECT ON SCHOOL ENROLLMENT RESIDENCY
A separately codified Education Code provision reinforces the affidavit's practical, no-court effect for school purposes: a pupil who lives in the home of a caregiving adult satisfies school-district residency requirements once that caregiving adult executes the Family Code § 6550 affidavit, and no guardianship or custody order is required for that determination, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the minor does not live with the caregiver.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A pupil who lives in the home of a caregiving adult that is located within the boundaries of that school district. Execution of an affidavit under penalty of perjury pursuant to Part 1.5 (commencing with Section 6550) of Division 11 of the Family Code by the caregiving adult is a sufficient basis for a determination that the pupil lives in the home of the caregiver, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the pupil is not living in the home of the caregiver."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 48204(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text), Educ. C. § 48204(a)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=48204)
  "Section 48204 of the Education Code provides that this affidavit constitutes a sufficient basis for a determination of residency of the minor, without the requirement of a guardianship or other custody order, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information), Fam. C. § 6552, To School Officials ¶1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6552)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a caregiver's affidavit — not a guardianship — can independently satisfy a school residency requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The school district retains authority to determine from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver, which can override this residency effect.

FORMAL COURT GUARDIANSHIP, IN CONTRAST TO THE AFFIDAVIT
Unlike the Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit, a legal guardianship of a minor's person or estate is established only through a court proceeding. A petition requesting appointment of a guardian must specify the proposed guardian's name and address, the proposed ward's name and date of birth, and must state that the appointment is necessary or convenient. At the hearing on that petition, the court — not the petition alone — decides whether to appoint a guardian of the person, the estate, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510)
  "Upon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1514(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1514)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a formal guardianship (unlike the affidavit mechanism) requires an actual court petition and hearing — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination, and not a description of the full court guardianship process, which involves additional notice, investigation, and ongoing court-oversight requirements not covered here.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

[Notary acknowledgment or witness signature lines, as applicable, attached.]

citations.quote: A pupil who lives in the home of a caregiving adult that is located within the boundaries of that school district. Execution of an affidavit under penalty of perjury pursuant to Part 1.5 (commencing with Section 6550) of Division 11 of the Family Code by the caregiving adult is a sufficient basis for a determination that the pupil lives in the home of the caregiver, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the pupil is not living in the home of the caregiver.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.quote: Section 48204 of the Education Code provides that this affidavit constitutes a sufficient basis for a determination of residency of the minor, without the requirement of a guardianship or other custody order, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a caregiver's affidavit — not a guardianship — can independently satisfy a school residency requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The school district retains authority to determine from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver, which can override this residency effect.

expectedJSON.body: Unlike the Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit, a legal guardianship of a minor's person or estate is established only through a court proceeding. A petition requesting appointment of a guardian must specify the proposed guardian's name and address, the proposed ward's name and date of birth, and must state that the appointment is necessary or convenient. At the hearing on that petition, the court — not the petition alone — decides whether to appoint a guardian of the person, the estate, or both.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Upon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a formal guardianship (unlike the affidavit mechanism) requires an actual court petition and hearing — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination, and not a description of the full court guardianship process, which involves additional notice, investigation, and ongoing court-oversight requirements not covered here.
